In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying the detection of chromatic stimuli in the primate visual system.
the neural mechanisms underlying the perception of color and the detection of chromatic stimuli.
the visual system's ability to detect and discriminate color, the mechanisms underlying this ability, and how these mechanisms change with age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the V1 neurons we studied were not tuned in any special way to the color directions used in our experiments.
the mechanisms underlying detection of chromatic contrast are not different in kind than those that underlie detection of luminance contrast.
V1 neurons respond to a diverse set of chromatic stimuli, but that the responses are too weak to account for detection behavior at threshold.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the V1 mechanisms of chromatic detection are not specialized for cardinal directions, but instead are broadly tuned to a wide range of color directions, and that the majority of neurons are unresponsive at threshold.

V1 neurons are tuned to the color directions that are most effective in driving the visual system, and that the most effective color directions differ for different animals and different experimental conditions.
the V1 population response is broadly distributed across the color space and that the monkey's chromatic detection threshold reflects the distribution of neuronal thresholds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
V1 is a highly diverse population of neurons that are not tuned to a few cardinal directions.
V1 neurons are generally less sensitive than the human visual system at detection threshold and, therefore, are unlikely to be the sole source of chromatic detection in the brain.
the relationship between V1 neural and psychophysical thresholds is not simple and that V1 is not a simple linear filter of color vision.
